blocks.text: One update improved the weight. But one step isn't enough. We need to do it over and over.
\text{calculate loss} \rightarrow \text{calculate gradient} \rightarrow \text{update weight} \rightarrow \text{repeat}
Each time through this loop is one step (or iteration). We keep going until the loss is small enough or we've done enough steps.

blocks.text: We've been predicting numbers. But a GAN's Discriminator predicts real or fake — a probability between 0 and 1. For that we need: Sigmoid activation and Binary Cross-Entropy loss.
Until now, we predicted numbers (delivery time = 13 minutes). But a GAN's Discriminator needs to predict real or fake -- a yes/no answer.
That's classification. And it needs two new tools.
Our neuron outputs any number: -5, 0, 3.7, 100...
But for "real or fake?" we need a number between 0 and 1:
How do we squash any number into the 0-1 range?
\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}
Don't worry about the formula. Just see what it does:
Three key facts:

items: Always between 0 and 1 -- perfect for probabilities
z = 0 -> output = 0.5 -- the midpoint
Smooth S-shape -- gradual transition, not a sudden jump

slides.title: Now we need a new loss function
slides.section: Now we need a new loss function

blocks.text: In Lesson 2, we used MSE (Mean Squared Error) for numbers.
For classification (0 or 1 targets), we use Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE):

slides.title: Now we need a new loss function
slides.section: Now we need a new loss function

blocks.text: BCE = -[y \cdot \log(p) + (1-y) \cdot \log(1-p)]
Where:

slides.title: Now we need a new loss function
slides.section: Now we need a new loss function

items: y = target (1 for real, 0 for fake)
p = sigmoid output (our predicted probability)

blocks.text: Both small -- good. But watch what happens with a very wrong prediction:
BCE punishes confident wrong answers much more than MSE. That's what we want for classification.
When target = 1 (real):
BCE = -\log(p)
The closer p is to 1, the smaller the loss:

steps: p ← 0.01  loss=4.6052    <-- very wrong, huge loss
p ← 0.99  loss=0.0101    <-- almost right, tiny loss

blocks.text: When target = 0 (fake):
BCE = -\log(1-p)
The closer p is to 0, the smaller the loss:

steps: p ← 0.01  loss=0.0101    <-- correctly says fake, tiny loss
p ← 0.99  loss=4.6052    <-- wrongly says real, huge loss
Discriminator updates to output lower p for fakes.
Generator updates to make fakes that get higher p.

blocks.text: This is the core of GAN training. Sigmoid + BCE make it work.

That was important for understanding. But real networks have millions of weights. Writing gradients by hand for all of them? Impossible.
PyTorch does the hard parts for you. You build the network. PyTorch calculates ALL the gradients automatically.
In NumPy, we used arrays. In PyTorch, we use tensors. Same idea -- just with superpowers.

In Lesson 6, we spent an entire lesson deriving gradient = 2 * error * input = 2 * (2-4) * 2 = -8.
PyTorch did it in one line.

d h ← d_pred * v                    # manual gradient step 3
d z ← d_h * (1 if z > 0 else 0)   # manual gradient step 4
grad w ← d_z * x                   # manual gradient step 5
